summary:
Other Space is a handmade model (diorama) of the Moon and Mars created by primary school students to tell the stories of the machines NASA left behind. Inside a cardboard box lit with LED lights, we built the Moon, Mars, a flag, a lander and a rocket, surrounded by the planets of the Solar System.

Our challenge, "Abandoned but not Forgotten", asks us to introduce school-age children to the hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars and the science it made possible. We started with Apollo 11: the base of the Eagle lunar module is still on the Moon, where it helped the first humans walk on another world. On Mars, we told the story of the Ingenuity helicopter, the first aircraft to make a powered flight on another planet, which completed 72 flights.

Our main message is that these machines are not just trash: they are the history of exploration. By building with our hands, children can see, touch and remember these stories.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Other Space is a physical storytelling model. It shows the Moon and Mars with representations of the machines NASA left there, so young children can learn about space exploration in a visual, hands-on way. It is presented together with a 30-second video and slides that explain each machine.

HOW WE MADE IT

- We read NASA resources about Apollo 11 and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

- We built the model with recycled cardboard, paper, paint, modeling paste and an LED light strip.

- We made slides in Canva to explain the Moon and Mars missions.

- We recorded the model and edited a short video with English subtitles.

THE STORIES WE TELL

- The Moon – Apollo 11 (1969): the Eagle lunar module carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the surface. Its descent stage is still at Tranquility Base.

- Mars – Ingenuity (2021–2024): the first helicopter on another planet. It was designed for 5 flights but completed 72, and it remains on Mars.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

The project helps children understand that every object left in space has a story and a scientific purpose. It encourages curiosity, respect for space history, and the idea that exploration should be done responsibly. It can be shown at school and in open classes for families.

TOOLS

Cardboard, paper, paint, LED lights, Canva (slides), a phone camera (video), and SI tools (Claude and Microsoft Copilot) for research, writing and video editing.

CREATIVITY

Instead of an app, we used our hands: a lit 3D model that turns NASA data into something children can see and touch.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Our audience is young children, so we used simple language, bright colors and short texts. We also checked our facts against NASA sources.
